title: Nonadaptive quantitative group testing
formal:
For every fixed real \(c\in(0,1)\), can a uniformly random set of \(k=\lfloor n^c\rfloor\) special items among \(n\) items be recovered exactly, with probability tending to one, from \(O(k)\) nonadaptive tests that each return the number of special items in a chosen subset?

Precisely, for each fixed \(c\in(0,1)\), do there exist a finite randomized testing-and-decoding algorithm \(A_c\), a constant \(C_c>0\), an integer \(n_c\), and a function \(\eta_c:\mathbb N\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\eta_c(n)=0\), such that the following holds for every integer \(n\ge n_c\)? Given \(n\) and \(k=\lfloor n^c\rfloor\), the algorithm chooses at most \(C_c k\) subsets \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\subseteq[n]\) before observing any test reply. The hidden set \(D\) is uniform among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), independently of the algorithm's coins. The reply to test \(j\) is the exact integer \(|Q_j\cap D|\). After receiving these replies, the algorithm returns a set \(\widehat D\) satisfying
\[\Pr_{D,A_c}[\widehat D=D]\ge1-\eta_c(n).\]
The test bound holds on every run. Test construction and decoding must terminate but have no prescribed time or space bound.

The answer to this query-count question is known to be yes. The selected target is therefore resolved; polynomial-time decoding is a separate additional requirement.
why: This problem separates the information obtained from a batch of count measurements from the computation needed to reconstruct the hidden items. Its affirmative query bound shows that nonadaptivity alone does not force an extra logarithmic factor in the sparse power-law regime. The distinction between count and Boolean measurements, and between information sufficiency and efficient decoding, is central to interpreting group-testing guarantees.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively for the user-selected count-valued subset-query target with unrestricted decoding. On 16 September 2026 this review inspected Feige and Lellouche, arXiv:2006.09074v1, §1 and Appendix A.3 Lemma 13, pp. 35–36: its pools form a binary Bernoulli matrix, and its growing-sparsity information-theoretic upper bound gives O(k) tests for every fixed power-law exponent. The full upper-bound argument was checked for the required model; the preprint is not represented as a peer-reviewed publication. The earlier Grebinski–Kucherov report was also inspected but its explicitly fixed-sparsity theorem is not alone used for the growing regime. Later multiset-query efficient-decoding results are distinguished. No polynomial decoding-time requirement was stated by the selected question, and this status makes no assertion that all efficient subset-decoding variants are resolved. No new mathematical theorem or Lean formalization is claimed.

progress.text: Grebinski and Kucherov formalize binary separating matrices for nonadaptive additive queries; the inspected report states its asymptotic theorem for fixed sparsity.
The WOLA problem page asks to close the nonadaptive query gap, with an inconsistency between its quantitative label and Boolean description.
Feige and Lellouche supply the binary-pool information-theoretic upper-bound proof for the growing sublinear regime and distinguish it from efficient decoding.
Hahn-Klimroth and Müller give near-optimal efficient decoding from pooled data in a multiset-query model.
The user-selected subset-count, unrestricted-decoding target is classified as resolved affirmatively after checking the binary matrix definition and the growing-regime upper-bound proof.

category_assignment.reason: The task is exact hidden-set identification from nonadaptive pooled queries, not deciding proximity to a property.

importance.reason: A fundamental pooled-measurement question connecting sparse recovery, nonadaptive experiments and information-versus-computation distinctions. The selected unrestricted query-count target is mathematically meaningful but has a checked affirmative resolution and belongs in the inactive archive.

sentences: Quantitative group testing identifies a hidden set from the exact number of its items in each tested subset.
The selected question fixes all tests before seeing replies and asks for exact recovery of a uniformly random sparse set with probability tending to one.
When the set size is a fixed power of the universe size, the target is a number of tests linear in the hidden-set size.
Binary-matrix information-theoretic bounds already achieve this target when decoding time is unrestricted.
The completed record is therefore resolved affirmatively, with efficient decoding and multiset tests explicitly distinguished.

definitions:
The item universe is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\) an integer at least two. The algorithm is given \(n\) and the exact integer \(k\) in binary. It is not given the hidden set or any information correlated with that set other than test replies. For each fixed \(c\in(0,1)\), the asymptotic sequence uses \(k=\lfloor n^c\rfloor\). Thus \(k\) tends to infinity while \(k/n\) tends to zero. The rounding convention removes the assumption that \(n^c\) happens to be an integer. The endpoint regimes of constant \(k\) and \(k\) proportional to \(n\) are outside the quantified target.

A test is an ordinary subset \(Q\) of the universe. Each item occurs in it either once or not at all. Its noiseless reply is \(|Q\cap D|\), an integer between zero and \(k\), including both endpoints. Subsets can have arbitrary sizes. There is no cost proportional to their cardinality, and no restriction on how many tests can contain one item. Repeating a test is allowed but each repetition counts as another test. Empty and full-universe tests are legal.

Equivalently, a list of \(m\) tests is a matrix \(B\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), where \(B_{ji}=1\) precisely when \(i\in Q_j\). If \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) is the indicator vector of \(D\), the reply vector is \(y=Bx\) with arithmetic over the integers. The algorithm knows its entire test matrix. Entries greater than one, weighted pools, arithmetic modulo two and replies reporting only whether an intersection is nonempty are different models and are not allowed here.

Nonadaptivity means that the entire list of tests, including its length, is determined by \(n,k\) and internal randomness before any reply is received. No test may depend on another test's reply. Decoding can inspect all replies and the test list, perform arbitrary finite computation and use further independent random bits, but it cannot ask additional tests beyond the preselected list. Nonadaptivity concerns the oracle queries; it does not impose a parallel running-time bound on the computation that prepares or decodes them.

The output is a subset of \([n]\), represented by its sorted list of distinct labels. Success means exact equality to the whole hidden set. Missing even one item or adding one false item is failure. A failure symbol or malformed output also counts as failure. Approximate recovery of almost all special items is not sufficient.

Probability is over a uniform hidden \(k\)-element set and all of the algorithm's independent fair random bits. The success guarantee is an average over that uniform distribution of hidden sets, as in the selected source target. It does not require a fixed deterministic design to recover every hidden set simultaneously. No adversary may choose the hidden set after seeing the random test design. An algorithm that succeeds for every fixed hidden set over its own coins gives a stronger admissible guarantee.

Use finite Turing-machine programs with exact binary integer computation and independent unbiased random bits. For each fixed \(c\), a single program \(A_c\) must handle all \(n\) in the stated sequence; there are no separate advice strings or free tables for each input length. The program may depend on the fixed regime \(c\), but \(c\) is not supplied as a real-number oracle: its actual inputs are the finite integers \(n,k\). A single program for all pairs \((n,k)\) would also suffice. Initialization, test selection and decoding must finish on every run. Their running time, memory, random-bit count, query-description length and output length are not the resource being optimized.

The measured cost is solely the number \(m\) of oracle tests. For every sufficiently large \(n\) in each fixed regime, every run must satisfy \(m\le C_c k\); an expected query bound alone would not suffice. The constants \(C_c,n_c\), the program and the rate \(\eta_c\) may depend on \(c\). They cannot depend on \(n\), the hidden set or the realized coins. There is no requirement that \(C_c\) stay bounded as \(c\) approaches zero or one. Failure tends to zero for each fixed \(c\); no particular polynomial rate is imposed.

The quantifier order is \(\forall c\in(0,1)\;\exists A_c,C_c,n_c,\eta_c\;\forall n\ge n_c\), followed by the stated random experiment with \(k=\lfloor n^c\rfloor\). The target asks whether a linear number of tests is attainable, rather than for the exact best leading constant or a complete optimal query function over all \((n,k)\).

Scope decision: the source uses the word quantitative but also describes yes/no replies. On 16 September 2026, the user selected quantitative count replies, nonadaptive subset tests and the \(O(k)\) recovery target in the power-law sparse regime. This card records that correction. Neither the brief question nor the selected target specifies polynomial-time reconstruction. No such extra condition is inserted. Later papers explicitly distinguish unrestricted reconstruction from efficient decoding, and some use multiset rather than subset tests; those distinctions affect which result answers the selected question.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence assertion, with the exact subset-count oracle, nonadaptivity, uniform hidden-set distribution, termination convention and fixed-regime quantifiers above. An affirmative proof must establish an \(O(k)\) worst-case test bound and failure probability tending to zero for every fixed \(c\in(0,1)\). A negative proof must negate that full assertion and cover arbitrary terminating procedures without an added computational restriction. A lower bound only for polynomial-time decoders, Boolean replies or a particular family of pools would not refute this target. The known affirmative result settles the mathematical query-count question; citing a paper does not replace the required Lean proof. No numerical tolerance relaxes exact set recovery, and identifying an exact optimal leading constant is not required.

source_formulation.text: Problem 95 asks to close the gap between the lower and upper query bounds for nonadaptive group testing in a sparse random-set regime. It labels the tests quantitative while describing yes/no replies. The user selected count-valued subset tests and a linear-in-k query target. This card makes that correction explicit and retains the absence of a prescribed decoding-time bound.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the 2019 question, with the user-selected count-reply interpretation

context_blocks.text: Pooling asks several items about their hidden membership through one observation. When a pool returns a count, it can convey more information than a Boolean positive/negative reply. Requiring every pool to be fixed in advance allows all measurements to be collected without waiting for earlier outcomes.

For the chosen regime, the information scale in the source \(k\log(n/k)/\log k\) is linear in \(k\), with constants depending on the fixed exponent \(c\). Thus an \(O(k)\) upper bound is the natural query-order target; this does not assert a universal leading constant across all sparsity regimes.

A separating binary matrix assigns different integer reply vectors to different allowed hidden sets. Grebinski and Kucherov develop this formalism for nonadaptive additive queries. The inspected 1997 report states its main separating-matrix asymptotic for fixed sparsity, so that statement alone is not used to certify the growing-sparsity target here.

Feige and Lellouche explicitly treat binary subset pools and the regime \(k=n^c\). Their Appendix A.3 gives a full information-theoretic upper bound of order \(k\log(n/k)/\log k\), with success tending to one for a fixed hidden vector over the random design. Unrestricted finite decoding therefore gives the required exact-recovery guarantee, including its average over a uniform hidden set.

The same paper separates this information-theoretic statement from its investigation of polynomial-time recovery. The resolution recorded here uses the former and makes no claim that the computational questions discussed in the paper have all been settled.

Gebhard and coauthors likewise distinguish the number of measurements needed for unrestricted inference from the number sufficient for their efficient reconstruction algorithm. Their own random design samples with replacement, permitting repeated contributions by one item to one reply. That is a broader measurement format than the binary subset model retained here.

The COLT 2022 efficient decoding result is relevant historical progress for pooled data, but its formal query model also uses multisets. It is not silently imported as a polynomial-time subset-test theorem. The unrestricted binary-matrix result already answers this card.
